questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis and regional lymphadenopathy consistent with primary syphilis. Which statement best explains why benzathine penicillin G maintains treponemicidal activity for 18–25 days despite the organism's slow division time?
opts: Penicillin achieves high cerebrospinal fluid penetration, allowing prolonged CNS coverage
The depot formulation provides continuous serum levels above the MIC (~0.018–0.1 mcg/mL) that suppress enzyme synthesis even during the organism's 30–33 hour division cycle
Benzathine penicillin undergoes rapid renal clearance, which paradoxically extends its half-life in infected tissues
The drug irreversibly binds to all bacterial cell wall proteins, eliminating the need for continuous exposure
questions.exp: Treponema pallidum divides extremely slowly (30–33 hours in early syphilis), so it requires prolonged, continuous penicillin exposure above its MIC to prevent recovery of enzyme synthesis. Benzathine penicillin's depot preparation maintains treponemicidal levels for 18–25 days, matching the prolonged division cycle. If levels drop below MIC, the organism can resume peptidoglycan synthesis within 20 minutes and escape death.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SNAIL (slow Treponema) being chased by a BENZATHINE GUARD patrolling a castle hallway for 18–25 DAYS straight—the guard never leaves (continuous MIC coverage), so the snail never escapes.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with scabies affecting multiple body areas including the face and scalp. Which topical agent is most appropriate for this patient?
opts: Permethrin 5% cream applied to entire body including face and scalp
Benzyl benzoate 10% emulsion applied for 24 hours
Precipitated sulfur 5% ointment applied overnight for 3 successive days
Crotamiton 10% cream applied for 5 consecutive nights
questions.exp: Precipitated sulfur 5–10% ointment is the treatment of choice for neonates <2 months of age and is safe for infants. Although permethrin is approved for infants >2 months and would normally include face/scalp coverage in this age group, precipitated sulfur is the safest option for the youngest infants. Benzyl benzoate is contraindicated in children <2 years due to neurotoxicity risk, and crotamiton has poor efficacy.

questions.q: A 17-year-old with confirmed EBV-induced infectious mononucleosis is prescribed ampicillin for what the clinician suspects is secondary bacterial pharyngitis. Seven days later, an intensely pruritic, bright red, confluent maculopapular rash develops on the trunk and upper extremities. Which statement regarding this ampicillin rash is most accurate?
opts: It represents a true Type I hypersensitivity reaction and contraindicates all future penicillin use
It is caused by EBV-induced polyclonal B-cell activation producing IgM antibodies against aminopenicillin, and does NOT preclude future penicillin use
It is a delayed-type IV hypersensitivity reaction requiring immediate cessation of the drug and desensitization therapy
It occurs in >95% of EBV patients given aminopenicillins and indicates severe immunosuppression
questions.exp: The ampicillin rash in IM is a transient virus-induced immunological cross-reaction, NOT a true penicillin allergy. EBV-driven polyclonal B-cell activation generates IgM antibodies against the aminopenicillin, forming immune complexes that trigger the maculopapular exanthem. This rash resolves with desquamation and does not preclude future penicillin use. Modern incidence is approximately 30% (historically 90–100%).
questions.source: EBV Cutaneous Manifestations (Infectious Mononucleosis, Ampicillin Rash, Gianotti-Crosti)
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In the castle hall, the EBV VIRUS RECRUITS a WILD PARTY OF B-CELLS who mass-produce ANTI-AMPICILLIN ANTIBODIES (like party crashers targeting the penicillin flag)—they form IMMUNE COMPLEX FIREWORKS that burst across the skin as a RASH, but it's NOT a true allergy, so the PENICILLIN BANNERS can still fly another day.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with early-onset poikiloderma, severe radial ray defects with hypoplastic thumbs, and imaging reveals a metaphyseal osteosarcoma. Genetic testing confirms compound heterozygous mutations in a DNA helicase gene on chromosome 8q24.3. Which of the following statements regarding this patient's molecular pathology is correct?
opts: The defective gene encodes APC1, a core component of the anaphase-promoting complex, and the patient has a low malignancy risk
The defective gene encodes RECQL4 DNA helicase essential for DNA replication initiation and UV damage removal, and the patient carries a 32% osteosarcoma risk
The defective gene encodes a transmembrane immunoglobulin receptor involved in autoimmune destruction of melanocytes
The disorder is primarily autoimmune-mediated with strong HLA associations requiring immunosuppressive therapy
questions.exp: This patient has Rothmund-Thomson Syndrome Type II driven by RECQL4 mutations on chromosome 8q24.3. RECQL4 encodes a DNA helicase essential for DNA replication initiation and efficient removal of UV-induced DNA damage. Type II patients classically present with severe skeletal abnormalities including radial ray defects and carry a massive 32% risk of developing osteosarcoma, alongside increased risk for cutaneous squamous cell and basal cell carcinomas. RTS is fundamentally a DNA repair disorder, NOT an autoimmune or immunobullous disease with no pathogenic autoantibodies or HLA associations.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's DNA LIBRARY on chromosome 8, a BROKEN HELICASE LADDER (RECQL4) blocks the repair workers from fixing UV-scorched scrolls—so OSTEOSARCOMA monsters (32% risk) storm through the RADIAL RAY portcullis.

questions.q: A dermatologist is counseling a 28-year-old woman with adult-onset acne about the biochemical alterations in her sebum composition. Compared to unaffected individuals, which lipid profile abnormality is characteristic of acne-prone sebum?
opts: Elevated linoleic acid and decreased squalene content
Elevated squalene and decreased linoleic acid content
Decreased free fatty acids with increased wax ester proportion
Elevated cholesterol esters with normal triglyceride levels
questions.exp: Sebum in acne patients contains higher levels of squalene and lower levels of linoleic acid, which promotes follicular hyperkeratinization and compromises the epidermal barrier. This qualitative alteration makes the follicle more permeable to inflammatory mediators.

questions.q: A pregnant woman with untreated syphilis is concerned about transmission to her fetus. Regarding transmission via blood transfusion, why is parenteral transmission of T. pallidum extremely rare despite the organism's presence in blood?
opts: T. pallidum is unable to survive the acidic environment of the gastrointestinal tract after transfusion
The organism dies in stored, refrigerated blood after 2 to 3 days at 4°C
Transfused blood is routinely sterilized by gamma radiation before administration
T. pallidum lacks the metabolic capacity to cross the blood–brain barrier
questions.exp: T. pallidum is exquisitely fragile and cannot survive desiccation, heating, or cold storage. In blood transfusions, the organism dies in refrigerated storage at 4°C within 2 to 3 days, making bloodborne transmission extremely rare. The other options are not relevant to the organism's survival in stored blood.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A FROZEN TREPONEME in a BLOOD BAG at 4°C becomes an ICE SCULPTURE—it perishes within 2–3 days in the refrigerator (unlike room-temperature bugs that survive longer)!

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with extensive molluscum contagiosum affecting the face and genitalia. Viral genome analysis reveals MCV II as the causative agent. Which immune evasion mechanism is specifically encoded by the MCV gene MC148R?
opts: Interleukin-18 binding and IFN-γ inhibition
Chemokine antagonism through viral homolog of cellular chemokines
Apoptosis inhibition via selenocysteine glutathione peroxidase
NF-κB pathway inhibition through death effector domains
questions.exp: The MC148R gene encodes a viral homolog of cellular chemokines that acts as an antagonist to block host chemokine activity. MC53L and MC54L bind IL-18 to inhibit IFN-γ production; MC66 contains selenocysteine glutathione peroxidase for apoptosis inhibition; and MC159 contains death effector domains for NF-κB inhibition.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: MC148R's CHEMICAL TWIN (chemokine homolog) masquerades as a fake GUARD at the castle gate, blocking all real chemokine messengers from entering.

questions.q: A 35-year-old immunocompromised patient is diagnosed with crusted scabies. Why is oral ivermectin combined with topical agents preferred over topical monotherapy?
opts: Oral ivermectin has excellent ovicidal activity and eliminates all mite eggs in a single dose
Oral ivermectin penetrates deeper into crusted lesions and reaches mites inaccessible to topical agents, though repeat dosing is required due to lack of ovicidal activity
Topical agents are ineffective in immunocompromised patients and oral ivermectin is the only active agent
Oral ivermectin prevents secondary bacterial infection better than permethrin
questions.exp: Oral ivermectin is first-line for crusted scabies because it achieves systemic penetration into heavily crusted areas where topical agents may not adequately reach the high mite burden. However, ivermectin lacks ovicidal activity, necessitating a second dose in 7–14 days to kill newly hatched larvae. Topical agents are still used concurrently to manage surface infestations.

questions.q: A genetic counselor is evaluating a family with X-linked recessive hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome). The mother is an asymptomatic carrier. What is the expected ratio of affected to unaffected males among her sons, and what is the pathophysiological basis for mild disease in some female carriers?
opts: 1:1 ratio; female carriers show mild disease due to skewed X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization)
3:1 ratio; female carriers show mild disease due to heterozygous advantage
All sons affected; female carriers are always asymptomatic due to X-linked dominant inheritance
1:3 ratio; female carriers show mild disease due to mitochondrial compensation
questions.exp: X-linked recessive inheritance predicts that sons of carrier mothers have a 1:1 ratio of affected to unaffected males. Female carriers may exhibit mild, patchy anhidrosis or missing teeth due to random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization), which results in mosaicism with some cells expressing the normal allele and others the mutant allele. More than 90% of severely affected individuals with this disorder are male.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated for hypopigmented streaks distributed along the lines of Blaschko on his limbs and torso. Physical examination shows no systemic abnormalities, normal neurological development, intact vision, and no skeletal defects. What is the most appropriate diagnosis for this patient?
opts: Hypomelanosis of Ito
Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation
Incontinentia Pigmenti Achromians
Vitiligo with linear distribution
questions.exp: By modern definition, Hypomelanosis of Ito is strictly reserved for patients with BOTH cutaneous pigmentation defects AND systemic/extracutaneous anomalies (CNS, musculoskeletal, ocular defects). This patient has only cutaneous findings without internal defects, making the correct diagnosis Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation. Incontinentia Pigmenti Achromians is an outdated misnomer that should no longer be used.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's SKIN GALLERY, pure hypopigmented STREAKS alone stand as a LONELY PORTRAIT (Linear Nevoid Hypopigmentation)—but when you add BRAIN PAINTINGS, BONE STATUES, and EYE SCULPTURES throughout the entire palace, THEN the collection becomes the complete HYPOMELANOSIS OF ITO MUSEUM.

questions.q: A 2-week-old term neonate born after maternal gestational diabetes develops firm, erythematous, non-mobile nodules on the cheeks, back, and buttocks. Blood work shows hypercalcaemia (12.5 mg/dL), elevated alkaline phosphatase, and elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Histology demonstrates lobular fat necrosis with a brisk chronic inflammatory infiltrate, preserved fat lobule architecture, and absence of vasculitis. Which of the following BEST distinguishes this condition from sclerema neonatorum?
opts: Sclerema neonatorum presents with circumscribed nodules, whereas subcutaneous fat necrosis causes diffuse board-like induration

Subcutaneous fat necrosis is associated with systemic hypercalcaemia and elevated vitamin D metabolites; sclerema neonatorum presents in critically ill premature infants with no metabolic abnormalities
Sclerema neonatorum is an autoimmune panniculitis; subcutaneous fat necrosis is a metabolic disorder
Subcutaneous fat necrosis occurs exclusively in post-term infants; sclerema neonatorum occurs in term neonates
questions.exp: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn typically affects term or post-term infants (often with maternal diabetes, birth trauma, or cold exposure) and is characterised by circumscribed nodules with brisk inflammation and a distinctive association with hypercalcaemia and elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. In contrast, sclerema neonatorum affects severely ill premature infants, causes diffuse woody induration with minimal inflammation, and lacks metabolic disturbances—the pathology is purely physical crystallisation of saturated fat.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine TWO ROYAL BABIES in the castle: SCLEREMA sits RIGID on the THRONE (premature, DIFFUSE, WOODEN, no calcium), while SUBCUTANEOUS FAT NECROSIS bounces around with NODULAR BUMPS (term baby, FOCAL, INFLAMED, HYPERGLYCAEMIA + HIGH VITAMIN D—like a CANDY STORE turned TOXIC).

questions.q: A 2-day-old full-term healthy neonate presents with scattered erythematous macules and firm 1–3 mm pustules with a characteristic 'flea-bitten' appearance on the trunk and face, sparing the palms and soles. A smear is taken from a pustule. Which finding on Wright–Giemsa staining would be most consistent with this diagnosis?
opts: Predominance of neutrophils with gram-positive cocci
Massive predominance of eosinophils with occasional neutrophils, sterile
Intracellular inclusion bodies and multinucleated giant cells
Budding yeast forms and pseudohyphae
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN) is characterized by a striking predominance of eosinophils (not neutrophils or organisms) on smear cytology, despite the clinical appearance of pustules—these are actually sterile eosinophilic collections. This finding helps distinguish ETN from neonatal herpes, bacterial infection, or candidiasis, which would show different cellular patterns or organisms.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Transient Neonatal Pustular and Vesicular Eruptions

questions.q: A 3-year-old girl presents with asymmetric whorled streaks of hypopigmentation on her trunk and extremities that follow the lines of Blaschko. Her parents report normal early development, but recent neuroimaging reveals cortical abnormalities. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological basis of this condition?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes mediated by pathogenic anti-melanocyte antibodies
Post-zygotic somatic mutation occurring early in embryogenesis leading to a clone of pigment-deficient skin cells
Immune complex deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction triggering complement activation
Genetic mutation inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern affecting all melanocytes systemically
questions.exp: Hypomelanosis of Ito is fundamentally a genetic mosaicism resulting from post-zygotic somatic mutations occurring early in embryogenesis, which create clones of melanocytes with decreased pigment synthesis capacity. This is NOT an autoimmune disorder and lacks HLA associations, pathogenic antibodies, or autoimmune serology findings. The condition is strictly a neurocutaneous dysplasia involving ectodermal and mesodermal structures.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SOMATIC CLONE ARMY marching through an EMBRYO CASTLE at dawn—each mutant cell drops its PIGMENT PAINTBRUSH as it migrates along BLASCHKO'S ROADS, leaving WHITE WHORLED FOOTPRINTS behind (NOT the immune-mediated autoimmune ambush from the gatehouse).

questions.q: A pregnant woman with secondary syphilis has documented IgE-mediated penicillin allergy. What is the evidence-based management approach before administering benzathine penicillin G?
opts: Administer ceftriaxone 1 g IM weekly for 3 weeks as a safe cross-reactive alternative
Use doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 28 days to avoid systemic penicillin exposure
Perform oral or intravenous penicillin desensitization with gradual micro-dose escalation to induce temporary tolerance, followed immediately by standard benzathine penicillin dosing
Administer azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for 14 days and monitor for neonatal outcome
questions.exp: Doxycycline and other non-penicillin alternatives are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy because they do not reliably prevent transplacental transmission of Treponema pallidum and risk fetal harm. Desensitization induces temporary tolerance by administering increasing micro-doses, allowing the allergic mother to receive the only truly effective agent (benzathine penicillin, ~98% effective at preventing congenital syphilis) while maintaining the pregnancy.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A PREGNANT QUEEN sits in the throne room refusing PENICILLIN due to allergy; a WISE ALCHEMIST slowly feeds her tiny increasing POTION DROPS at the COURTYARD WELL until she builds TOLERANCE, then delivers the GOLDEN CURE (benzathine penicillin) to save both MOTHER and BABY.

questions.q: A 5-year-old girl with poikiloderma and bilateral cataracts develops recurrent respiratory infections but shows no malignancy on long-term follow-up. Genetic testing reveals homozygous mutations in the ANAPC1 gene on chromosome 2q13. Which molecular target and clinical outcome most accurately define this patient's condition?
opts: RECQL4 DNA helicase deficiency with 32% osteosarcoma predisposition and skeletal abnormalities
ANAPC1 deficiency affecting anaphase-promoting complex function with NO increased malignancy incidence but high cataract risk
APC tumor suppressor loss with familial adenomatous polyposis and guaranteed colorectal malignancy
Autoimmune destruction of lens proteins mediated by anti-lens crystallin autoantibodies with HLA-DR4 association
questions.exp: This patient has Rothmund-Thomson Syndrome Type I caused by ANAPC1 mutations on chromosome 2q13. ANAPC1 encodes a core component of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome critical for cell cycling, senescence, and DNA repair. Type I patients present with classic poikiloderma and are uniquely distinguished by a HIGH INCIDENCE OF JUVENILE CATARACTS (the original Rothmund presentation) but crucially have NO increased incidence of malignancy, contrasting sharply with Type II. RTS is an inherited genomic instability disorder, not an autoimmune process.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's CELL CYCLE BALLROOM on chromosome 2, the BROKEN APC DANCE PARTNER (ANAPC1) tangles the CATARACT CHANDELIER (juvenile cataracts glow above), but the CANCER DRAGONS sleep soundly—Type I's cancer-sparing SHIELD protects the realm.

questions.q: A 16-year-old male presents with comedonal acne on his face. Histopathologically, the initial subclinical precursor lesion before all acne manifestations is identified. Which structural abnormality characterizes this earliest lesion?
opts: Increased sebaceous gland size with elevated triglyceride production
Microcomedo formation due to abnormal hyperkeratinization in the infrainfundibulum
Bacterial colonization of the follicle by Cutibacterium acnes
Perifollicular inflammatory infiltrate with neutrophil predominance
questions.exp: The microcomedo is the initial, subclinical precursor to all acne lesions. It results from abnormal hyperkeratinization in the infrainfundibulum where increased keratinocyte proliferation and retention with persistent desmosomes cause a bottleneck phenomenon and failure of normal desquamation.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with a geographic port-wine stain on his left lower limb, asymmetric limb hypertrophy, and varicose veins on imaging. There are NO arteriovenous fistulae or high-flow shunting detected. Which of the following best describes the genetic basis of his condition?
opts: Germline gain-of-function mutation in PIK3CA inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
Postzygotic somatic gain-of-function mutation in PIK3CA causing PI3K/AKT/mTOR hyperactivation restricted to the lesional clone
Loss-of-function mutation in RASA1 affecting RAS signaling uniformly across all tissues
Germline heterozygous mutation in VG5Q causing angiogenic factor deficiency
questions.exp: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome is caused by a postzygotic somatic gain-of-function mutation in PIK3CA (encoding p110α of PI3K) that arises after fertilization and remains confined to the affected tissue clone, not the germline. This somatic mosaicism allows survival, whereas the same mutation would be embryonically lethal if present throughout the germline (Happle's lethal mutation hypothesis). The mutation drives constitutive hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, the master regulator of growth, proliferation, and angiogenesis.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with fine, white-to-gray flaky scales predominantly on the extensor surfaces of his elbows and knees. His palms show prominent hyperlinearity, and he has a personal history of asthma. Which genetic defect is most likely responsible for his condition?
opts: Loss-of-function mutation in the FLG gene encoding filaggrin
Deletion of the STS gene causing steroid sulfatase deficiency
Mutation in the ABCA12 gene encoding an ATP-binding cassette transporter
Defect in transglutaminase-1 causing lamellar ichthyosis
questions.exp:
Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the FLG gene on chromosome 1q21, which encodes filaggrin—a critical protein for keratin aggregation and synthesis of natural moisturizing factors in the stratum corneum. The clinical triad of fine scales favoring extensors, hyperlinear palms, and atopic diathesis is pathognomonic for this autosomal dominant disorder.
🏰 Palace: Picture FILAGGRIN as a FABRIC FITTER in the castle's GRANULOSUM GRAND HALL—when she's fired (FLG loss), white FLAKES fall everywhere on the EXTENSOR WALKWAY, but never visit the FLEXURE TOWERS.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on his penis. Dark field microscopy is ordered. Which structural feature of Treponema pallidum allows it to evade the host immune system most effectively during early infection?
opts: High lipopolysaccharide (LPS) content in the outer membrane
Outer membrane that completely lacks LPS and contains 100-fold fewer integral transmembrane proteins than typical gram-negative bacteria
Presence of multiple axial filaments that mask antigenic epitopes
Production of a thick peptidoglycan layer that prevents antibody penetration
questions.exp: T. pallidum's outer membrane is antigenically inert because it completely lacks lipopolysaccharide endotoxin and has 100-fold fewer integral transmembrane proteins than typical gram-negative bacteria. This minimal surface antigenicity is a critical immune evasion strategy that allows the organism to establish infection before host antibodies develop. The axial filaments are responsible for motility, not immune evasion, and T. pallidum lacks a peptidoglycan layer.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a NAKED TREPONEMAL GHOST (no LPS coat) sneaking through the castle's IMMUNE GUARD STATION—it has so few door handles (proteins) that guards can't spot it!

questions.q: A 6-month-old male presents with recurrent episodes of unexplained fever and inability to sweat despite ambient temperatures of 32°C. Physical examination reveals a depressed nasal bridge, large lips, frontal bossing, and sparse fuzzy hair. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the EDA gene. What is the pathophysiological basis of this disorder?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of eccrine sweat glands mediated by pathogenic IgG antibodies
Primary inherited genetic developmental disorder affecting ectodermal structures due to defective ectodysplasin-A signaling
HLA-associated immune complex deposition in sweat gland basement membranes
Acquired immunodeficiency leading to selective loss of sweat gland innervation
questions.exp: Anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is a primary inherited genetic developmental disorder NOT mediated by autoimmunity, pathogenic antibodies, or HLA associations. The EDA gene encodes ectodysplasin A, a signaling molecule essential for embryologic development of ectodermal derivatives including eccrine sweat glands. Mutations in this pathway disrupt gland formation during development rather than destroying them post-natally.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about erythema toxicum neonatorum is CORRECT?
opts: It is caused by maternal lymphocytes transferred to the infant and is mediated by graft-versus-host responses
It typically presents within the first 6–12 hours of life and persists for several weeks
It is a common, benign, self-limiting eruption affecting 48–72% of full-term infants, rarely present at birth but classically beginning 24–48 hours after delivery
It is almost exclusively seen in premature and low-birth-weight neonates under 2500 g
questions.exp: ETN is one of the most common neonatal eruptions, affecting nearly half of all full-term healthy infants, and characteristically appears 24–48 hours after birth (not at delivery). The historical graft-versus-host hypothesis has been disproven; ETN is now understood as a localized innate-immune response to commensal skin microbes colonizing the infant's skin after birth.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Transient Neonatal Pustular and Vesicular Eruptions

questions.q: Which single clinical finding is the MANDATORY criterion that distinguishes Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome from Parkes-Weber syndrome?
opts: Presence of a port-wine stain (capillary malformation)
Progressive limb hypertrophy and soft-tissue overgrowth
Complete absence of high-flow arteriovenous fistulae or arterial shunts (slow-flow malformation only)
Involvement of the lower extremity rather than the upper extremity
questions.exp: Both Klippel-Trenaunay and Parkes-Weber syndromes can present with a port-wine stain and limb hypertrophy, making them phenotypically similar. However, the critical diagnostic distinction is that KTS is strictly a slow-flow combined capillary-lymphatic-venous malformation, while Parkes-Weber is characterized by underlying high-flow arteriovenous fistulae or malformations. The complete absence of fast-flow arterial shunts is mandatory for KTS diagnosis and is the key differentiator between the two conditions.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with a round, punched-out defect on the scalp vertex covered by a thin, translucent epithelial membrane. On examination, you note a ring of dark, coarse hair radially oriented around the lesion. What is the most likely morphological subtype and associated finding?
opts: Non-membranous ACC with cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita
Membranous ACC with a pathognomonic hair collar sign suggesting possible underlying neural tube defect
Stellate ACC with hypertrophic scarring requiring urgent surgical intervention
Epidermolytic ACC associated with mutations in the NOTCH1 gene
questions.exp: Membranous ACC presents classically as a round or oval, punched-out defect covered by a thin, shiny, translucent epithelial membrane. The pathognomonic 'hair collar sign'—a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair surrounding the lesion—is a clinical marker that can indicate an underlying neural tube defect. This morphological presentation results from incomplete closure of embryonic ectodermal fusion lines.

questions.q: A 19-year-old university student presents with fever, exudative pharyngitis, and tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. On examination, you note petechiae at the junction of hard and soft palate and bilateral periorbital puffiness. A rapid EBV test is positive. Which mechanism best explains the periorbital edema (Hoagland's sign) in this patient?
opts: Direct viral invasion of periorbital adipose tissue causing local inflammation
Lymphatic obstruction from profound lymphadenopathy impeding fluid drainage
Immune complex deposition in periorbital dermal vasculature triggering edema
Viral reactivation in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
questions.exp: Hoagland's sign (periorbital edema in IM) occurs as a consequence of profound lymphadenopathy causing mechanical lymphatic obstruction rather than direct viral infection or vasculitis. This sign is highly suggestive of IM and appears in approximately 50% of cases during the first week of illness.
questions.source: EBV Cutaneous Manifestations (Infectious Mononucleosis, Ampicillin Rash, Gianotti-Crosti)
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SWOLLEN FACE in a castle throne room—the GIANT LYMPH NODES in the neck (like castle gatekeepers) are BLOCKING the drainage tunnels beneath the EYES, causing facial puffiness to pile up like backed-up moat water.

questions.q: A 2-week-old male neonate presents with thick, dark-brown, polygonal scales with a characteristic 'dirty neck' appearance. His mother reports she experienced prolonged labor with this pregnancy. Genetic testing reveals a deletion on Xp22.3. Which systemic complication should this child be screened for in adulthood?
opts: Asymptomatic corneal opacities and cryptorchidism
Progressive sensory neuropathy and cardiac arrhythmias
Hepatomegaly and immune deficiency
Hypertension and renal insufficiency
questions.exp:
Recessive X-linked ichthyosis (RXLI) is caused by STS gene deletion on Xp22.3, leading to steroid sulfatase deficiency and cholesterol sulfate accumulation. Approximately 50% of affected males develop asymptomatic comma-shaped corneal opacities on the posterior capsule, and there is a 20-fold increased risk of cryptorchidism with independent risk for testicular cancer.
🏰 Palace: Imagine STEROID SULFATASE guards sitting at the XMAS (X-linked) castle CHECKPOINT—when they abandon duty (STS deletion), DIRTY CHOLESTEROL SCALES pile up on the NECK, and naughty TESTIS FAIRIES hide in their CRYPTIC LAIR while COMMA-shaped CRYSTALS coat the CORNEAL CRYSTAL BALL.

questions.q: A 3-day-old premature male infant with septicaemia and severe hypothermia presents with rapid-onset, diffuse, board-like induration of the skin starting on the buttocks and spreading symmetrically across the body. Palms and soles are spared. Histology shows fat necrosis with doubly refractile needle-shaped clefts arranged radially within adipocytes and thickened connective tissue septa, but minimal inflammatory infiltrate. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying this presentation?
opts: Immune-mediated destruction of adipocytes triggered by neonatal pathogens
Crystallization and solidification of subcutaneous fat due to immature lipolytic mechanisms and peripheral circulatory collapse in response to severe systemic stress
Lobular panniculitis with vasculitis of small arteries and veins supplying the subcutaneous tissue
Traumatic rupture of adipocytes secondary to intrauterine compression and birth trauma
questions.exp: Sclerema neonatorum results from the high saturated fatty acid content of neonatal fat and immature enzymatic lipolytic mechanisms. When a severely stressed premature infant experiences peripheral circulatory collapse and skin temperature drop, the fat cannot be mobilized and undergoes rapid crystallization. The pathognomonic doubly refractile needle-shaped clefts represent dissolved triglyceride crystals within adipocytes, and the sparse inflammation excludes vasculitic or immune-mediated mechanisms.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a PREMATURE BABY sitting in an ICY CASTLE THRONE—his saturated FAT CRYSTALLIZES like ICE SCULPTURES (needle clefts), his CIRCULATION COLLAPSES, and he turns into a FROZEN WOODEN BOARD from toes to chest (sparing palms/soles). The kingdom is in SEPTIC CHAOS (50–75% mortality).

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with multiple discrete, umbilical papules on the trunk and arms. The parents report the lesions appeared 8 weeks ago after the child attended summer camp. Which molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) subtype is most likely responsible for this infection?
opts: MCV II, which accounts for 80% of pediatric infections
MCV I, which is the predominant subtype in children and represents 76–97% of global infections
MCV III, which is the most common cause of childhood molluscum contagiosum
MCV IV, which preferentially infects the epidermis of immunocompetent children
questions.exp: MCV I is the most prevalent subtype globally, responsible for 76–97% of infections and is the predominant cause in children. MCV II is relatively more common in adults, particularly in sexual transmission and HIV-infected individuals. MCV III and IV are rare subtypes.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A CHILD sits at the FRONT (I) of a grand castle banquet table, claiming 76–97% of all treats—MCV I rules the kid kingdom.

questions.q: A 3-week-old infant with large, irregular midline scalp defects, prominent dilated scalp veins overlying a skull ossification defect, and bilateral shortened digits with syndactyly is evaluated. Which genetic mutation and syndrome classification best explains this clinical presentation?
opts: BMS1 mutation causing Group 1 scalp ACC without multiple anomalies
ARHGAP31 or NOTCH1 mutations causing Adams-Oliver Syndrome (Group 2 ACC with limb reduction defects)
EOGT mutation causing cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita without skeletal involvement
Autoimmune-mediated disease with HLA associations requiring immunosuppressive therapy
questions.exp: Adams-Oliver Syndrome (Group 2 ACC) is characterized by large, irregular, non-membranous midline scalp defects with dilated scalp veins and underlying skull ossification defects, combined with terminal transverse limb defects (shortened digits, syndactyly). This syndrome can result from autosomal dominant mutations in genes such as ARHGAP31, RBPJ, NOTCH1, or DLL4. ACC is a structural developmental anomaly, not an autoimmune or antibody-mediated disease, so HLA associations do not apply.
